unit.title: Apply knowledge of the history of massage

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Describe how massage was used in ancient China, India and Japan.
essays.modelAnswer: In ancient China, massage was part of traditional medicine for thousands of years, and old medical texts, such as the Yellow Emperor's Classic of Internal Medicine, describe it. The old word anmo means 'press and rub', and the later style tui na means 'push and grasp'. Chinese massage is based on the idea that life energy, called qi, flows along channels called meridians, and that pressing and rubbing help it to flow and keep the body in balance. In India, massage is part of Ayurveda, the traditional medicine. Warm oils, often with herbs, are massaged into the body, as in abhyanga, and head massage with oil has long been part of family grooming. In Japan, doctors learned Chinese methods, which became a massage called anma. In the 1900s, shiatsu, meaning 'finger pressure', grew from anma. It uses pressure from the thumbs, fingers and palms on special points, usually through the clothes.
markingPoints: China: part of traditional medicine for thousands of years (anmo, tui na)
China: based on the idea of qi flowing along meridians
India: Ayurveda, with warm herbal oils (abhyanga), and head massage as family grooming
Japan: anma, learned from Chinese methods
Japan: shiatsu ('finger pressure') grew from anma in the 1900s, using thumb, finger and palm pressure

essays.stem: Describe how massage was used in ancient Greece and Rome, and name at least one doctor of that time who wrote about it.
essays.modelAnswer: In ancient Greece, athletes were rubbed with olive oil before training and before the games, and afterwards they scraped off the oil, sweat and dust with a curved tool called a strigil. Massage was also part of medicine. Hippocrates, often called the father of medicine, wrote that a doctor must be skilled in 'anatripsis', or rubbing. He taught that rubbing could loosen a stiff joint or firm up a loose one. In ancient Rome, massage was often given at the public baths, after bathing, to relax and clean the body, and wealthy Romans made it part of their routine. Galen, a Greek-born doctor who worked in the Roman Empire and treated gladiators, wrote about massage before and after exercise and for keeping healthy. Their ideas were later kept alive and added to by Arab and Persian doctors, such as Ibn Sina.
markingPoints: Greek athletes rubbed with oil before training and the games (a strigil scraped it off)
Hippocrates: a doctor must be skilled in rubbing (anatripsis)
Hippocrates: rubbing can loosen a stiff joint or firm a loose one
Rome: massage at the public baths, after bathing
Galen wrote about massage with exercise and for health (or another correct doctor and idea)

essays.stem: Explain how massage developed in Europe in the 1800s, and why many of its strokes have French names.
essays.modelAnswer: In the early 1800s, Per Henrik Ling, a Swede, developed a system of health exercises called medical gymnastics. It included exercises the client did, movements the therapist did to the client, and massage strokes. He set up a teaching institute in Stockholm, and his ideas spread across Europe. He is often called the father of Swedish massage. Later in the 1800s, Johann Mezger, a Dutch doctor, studied massage in a scientific way and used it to treat patients with injuries and stiff joints. He used French words to name the strokes: effleurage (to skim lightly), petrissage (to knead) and tapotement (to tap). Doctors across Europe and America copied his methods and his words, which is why the classic strokes still have French names today. Massage became a hospital treatment, and in 1894 trained masseuses in Britain formed a society to set standards.
markingPoints: Ling (Sweden, early 1800s) developed medical gymnastics, with movements and massage
Ling is often called the father of Swedish massage, and his ideas spread across Europe
Mezger, a Dutch doctor, used massage in a scientific way to treat patients
Mezger named the strokes in French (effleurage, petrissage, tapotement), and others copied him
Massage became a hospital treatment, with standards set by trained masseuses in the late 1800s

essays.stem: Explain why massage became less used in hospitals in the 1900s, and why it became popular again later.
essays.modelAnswer: In the late 1800s and early 1900s, massage was an important hospital treatment. Trained masseuses treated injuries, and in the First World War they helped wounded soldiers to recover. In the middle of the 1900s, massage became less used in hospitals. Electrical machines, new medicines and exercise-based treatments took over much of the work, and physiotherapy, the profession that grew from the masseuses, used less hands-on massage. Massage also still had a poor name in some places, because of the improper 'massage' houses of the past. From the 1960s and 1970s, interest grew again. People became more interested in wellness, stress relief and natural, holistic care, and they looked to traditions from Asia. Spas and hotels began to offer massage, and sports teams used it for athletes. Today, in Jamaica and around the world, massage is popular in spas, hotels and clinics for relaxation and wellbeing.
markingPoints: Massage was a hospital treatment in the late 1800s and early 1900s (for example, for wounded soldiers)
Less used in the mid-1900s, as machines, medicines and exercise treatments took over
Physiotherapy used less hands-on massage, and massage still had a poor name in places
Revival from the 1960s–70s: interest in wellness, stress relief and holistic care
Spread into spas, hotels and sport, as it is today

essays.stem: Compare the Eastern and Western approaches to massage.
essays.modelAnswer: Eastern massage, such as Chinese tui na, Japanese shiatsu, Thai massage and Indian Ayurvedic massage, grew from traditional medicine that is thousands of years old. It is based on the idea of life energy flowing along channels or lines in the body, and it aims to keep that energy balanced. It often uses pressure on points and lines, stretches and rhythmic pressure, and it is often given through the clothes on a mat or futon, although Ayurvedic massage uses plenty of oil. Western massage, such as Swedish massage, grew from Ling's and Mezger's work in Europe in the 1800s. It is based on anatomy and physiology: the muscles, the blood and lymph circulation, and the nerves. It uses the classic strokes, such as effleurage, petrissage and tapotement, usually with oil on bare skin, on a couch, with towel draping. Both aim to relax the client and improve wellbeing, both need a consultation first, and many spas now mix them.
markingPoints: Eastern: from ancient traditional medicine (China, Japan, Thailand, India)
Eastern: based on energy flowing along channels or lines; pressure on points, and stretches
Eastern: often through the clothes on a mat (Ayurvedic massage uses oil)
Western: Swedish massage from 1800s Europe, based on anatomy and circulation, classic strokes with oil on a couch
Similarities: relaxation and wellbeing, a consultation first, often mixed in spas

essays.stem: Describe three massage styles from different parts of the world that might be offered in a Jamaican spa. For each one, give its origin and its main features.
essays.modelAnswer: Swedish massage comes from Europe in the 1800s, from Per Henrik Ling's movement work in Sweden and Johann Mezger's work in the Netherlands. It uses oil on bare skin and the classic strokes: effleurage, petrissage, tapotement, friction and vibration. The client lies on a couch, draped with towels. It suits clients who want to relax or ease tight muscles. Thai massage comes from Thailand and was shaped by Indian medicine and Buddhist practice. It is given on a mat, with the client in loose clothes and no oil. The therapist uses pressure along energy lines and gentle stretches. It suits clients who feel stiff and like stretching. Indian head massage comes from India, where head massage with oils was part of family grooming. The client sits in a chair, and the therapist massages the upper back, shoulders, neck, scalp and face, often with oil. It suits busy clients with tension in the neck and shoulders, and needs little undressing.
markingPoints: Names three styles from different parts of the world
Gives the correct origin of each style
Gives the correct main features of each (position, clothing, oil, movements)
Says who each style suits
Descriptions are accurate and clear enough for a client to understand

essays.stem: Explain what the history of massage in the late 1800s teaches today's therapists about a professional manner, training and standards.
essays.modelAnswer: In the late 1800s in Britain, the word 'massage' was misused by some places that were not real treatment rooms, and some untrained people offered it. This gave massage a bad name and made doctors and the public distrust it. In 1894, a group of trained women masseuses set up a society to protect their work. They set training and examinations, kept a list of qualified members, made rules about how members must behave, and worked only with patients sent by doctors. Their society later grew into the profession of physiotherapy. This teaches today's therapists that the good name of massage depends on each one of them. A professional manner, proper training and recognised qualifications such as NVQ-J, clear boundaries, correct draping, honest descriptions of treatments, a consultation and records, and following a code of conduct all show clients and the public that massage is a safe and respectable treatment.
markingPoints: The problem in the 1800s: misuse of the word 'massage' and untrained people gave it a bad name
Trained masseuses formed a society in 1894 (it grew into physiotherapy)
They set training, examinations and rules of conduct, and worked with doctors
Lesson: each therapist's behaviour and training protect the good name of massage
Today: professional manner, qualifications, boundaries, draping, honest claims, consultation and records

essays.stem: A client asks you where her treatment comes from, and whether it will cure her back problem. Explain how you would answer her, and why.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would answer her question about where the treatment comes from, simply and accurately. For a Swedish massage, for example, I would say that it grew from movement and massage work in Sweden and Europe in the 1800s, and that its strokes have French names. I would not make up stories or exaggerate how old the treatment is. Then I would be honest about her back. I would explain that massage can help her relax, ease tight muscles and feel more comfortable, but that it is not a cure, and that I cannot diagnose what is wrong with her back. If her back pain is new or severe, or comes with other signs such as numbness, I would advise her to see her doctor first, and I would note it on the consultation form. Answering in this way is honest and keeps within my training. It protects the client from harm, keeps her trust, and protects the good name of the salon and of massage.
markingPoints: Gives a simple, accurate account of where the treatment comes from
Does not exaggerate or make up history
Explains honestly what massage can do (relax, ease tight muscles) and that it is not a cure
Does not diagnose; refers to a doctor for new, severe or unusual pain, and records it
Says why: honesty, working within training, client safety and trust

essays.stem: Describe traditions of rubbing and massage with oils in Africa and the Caribbean, and how a Jamaican therapist can respect them in her work.
essays.modelAnswer: In many African cultures, massage with oils and shea butter has long been part of daily life, especially for babies and for mothers after childbirth, and for easing tired muscles. Many of these traditions came to the Caribbean with African people and mixed with other influences. In many Jamaican homes, older family members rub aches and pains with oils, such as castor oil or coconut oil, sometimes with local herbs, and babies are often oiled and rubbed after a bath. These traditions show that touch and oils for comfort and care are part of our own culture, not only something from abroad. A Jamaican therapist can respect them by speaking about them with pride and accuracy, and by using local oils only when she knows they are safe and has checked the client for allergies. She should not make medical claims for herbs, and she should always follow the consultation, hygiene and contraindication rules of the trade.
markingPoints: African traditions of massage with oils or shea butter, for example for babies, new mothers or tired muscles
These traditions came to the Caribbean and mixed with other influences
Jamaican home traditions of rubbing with oils such as castor or coconut oil
Respects them by speaking of them with pride and accuracy
Uses local oils safely: allergy checks, no medical claims, the usual consultation and hygiene rules

essays.stem: Explain how modern massage practice keeps what was good from the past, and what protections for clients it adds.
essays.modelAnswer: Modern massage keeps many good things from the past. It still uses the hands to press, rub and knead, as the ancient Chinese, Indians and Greeks did. It still uses oils, as in Ayurveda and in Greece and Rome, and many spas offer traditional styles, such as shiatsu, Thai massage and Indian head massage. The classic strokes still carry the French names from the 1800s. Modern practice also adds protections for clients. There is a consultation before every treatment, with checks for contraindications and referral to a doctor when needed. The client gives informed consent and can stop the treatment at any time. Towels are used to drape the client, so that only the area being worked is uncovered. Hygiene rules, such as hand washing, fresh towels and clean oil, stop infection. Records are kept confidential. Therapists are trained and assessed for qualifications, such as NVQ-J, and follow a professional code of conduct.
markingPoints: Keeps hands-on pressing, rubbing and kneading from ancient times
Keeps the use of oils and traditional styles, and the classic stroke names from the 1800s
Adds a consultation, contraindication checks and referral
Adds informed consent and draping
Adds hygiene rules, confidential records, training and qualifications

practical1.title: Illustrated timeline of the history of massage (group poster)
practical1.brief: As a group, make a large illustrated timeline poster of the history of massage, from ancient times to massage in Jamaica today. First, plan together and agree at least 12 events or periods to show, for example ancient China, India, Egypt, Greece and Rome, Persia, Japan, Ling in Sweden, the French names for the strokes, the masseuses' society of 1894, the World Wars, the revival from the 1970s, Thai and Hawaiian styles, and spa massage in Jamaica today. Share them out so that each member researches and writes at least 3 entries, using the Centre's library, class notes and the assessor's fact sheet. Each entry gives the date or period, the place, what happened and why it matters to a therapist today, in your own words, with a simple drawing or picture. Check each other's facts before writing them on the poster. Each member also takes one job: planning the layout, checking the facts, drawing, or leading the presentation. Finally, present the timeline to the assessor, with each member explaining their own entries. Photograph each stage below. Hand in once for the whole group, with the planning sheet and research notes.
materials: Large poster paper or card (or several sheets taped together)
Markers, coloured pencils, rulers, glue and scissors
Printed pictures or old magazines to cut up, if the Centre allows
Centre library books, class notes and the assessor's fact sheet
A planning sheet and a fact-check list
Sticky notes for the draft layout
photos: The planning sheet, with the events shared out and each member's name
Members' research notes for their entries
The draft layout on sticky notes
The poster half-way through, with entries being added
Each member presenting their entries beside the poster (faces only if the members agree and the Centre allows it)
The fact-check list, signed by the member who checked it
checklist: Took part in the planning and agreed a fair share of the events
Researched at least 3 entries, using reliable sources
Wrote each entry correctly: the date or period, the place, what happened and why it matters today
Wrote in their own words, clearly and neatly
Checked facts with the group and corrected any mistakes
Added a suitable picture or drawing for each entry
Explained their entries clearly in the presentation and answered a question
Worked well with the group and carried out their job
safety: Use scissors and glue carefully, and keep the work area tidy
Use only reliable sources, and check facts against the assessor's fact sheet
Do not copy pictures or text that the Centre's rules do not allow
Take photos only with the members' agreement, following the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Spa treatment menu with the origin of each massage, and a client explanation role play
practical2.brief: As a group, write and design a one-page treatment menu for the spa of a Jamaican hotel, offering at least five massage styles from different traditions (for example Swedish massage, shiatsu, Thai massage, Indian head massage, lomi lomi, aromatherapy massage or hot stone massage). For each treatment, the menu gives: its name; where it comes from, with one short, accurate line of history; what the client can expect (couch or mat, clothes on or oil on bare skin, the main movements); who it suits; and a reminder that a consultation is done first. Make no promise that a treatment cures illness. Each member writes at least one menu entry, and the group checks every entry for accuracy and plain language. Then hold a role play at a spa reception: each member, in turn, plays the therapist and explains one treatment on the menu to a 'client' (another member), and answers one question from the assessor's question cards, such as 'Will this cure my bad back?' or 'Is this really thousands of years old?'. The other members note on an observation sheet how honest, clear and professional each answer was. Photograph each stage below. Hand in once for the whole group, with the menu, the drafts and the observation sheets.
materials: Paper or card for the menu, or a computer with a printer
Centre library books, class notes and the assessor's fact sheet
The assessor's question cards for the role play
A table and two chairs set up as a spa reception
photos: The group's plan, showing which member writes each entry
The draft menu entries, with the group's corrections
The spa reception set up for the role play
Each role play in progress (hands and menu only, or faces if the members agree and the Centre allows it)
checklist: Wrote at least one accurate menu entry: name, origin, a line of history, what to expect and who it suits
Used plain, honest language, with no claim that massage cures illness
Included a reminder about the consultation and contraindications
Checked other members' entries and helped correct mistakes
In the role play, explained the treatment's origin clearly and accurately
Answered the client's question honestly, within their training, and referred to a doctor where needed
Kept a polite, professional manner throughout
Filled in the observation sheet fairly for other members
safety: Make no medical claims on the menu or in the role play
Use only reliable sources, and check facts against the assessor's fact sheet
If a movement is shown on a partner, do it only on a clothed forearm, with the partner's consent
Take photos only with the members' agreement, following the Centre's rules
